title: How a database stores data
problem: A query that touches one 100-byte row still reads whole pages from disk, and the wrong layout or engine turns a simple report into a full-table crawl.
summary: A storage engine moves fixed-size pages between disk and a buffer pool. Row stores suit transactions, column stores suit analytics, and MySQL, MongoDB and RocksDB show that the engine is a swappable part beneath the query layer.
catTip: I never fetch one kibble; I knock the whole bowl over. Databases are the same: ask for one row and a whole 8 kB page comes along. Keep the bowls you use most in the warm spot by the server.

recall.q: Why does a database read pages rather than rows, and what does the buffer pool do about the cost?
recall.a: Disks and SSDs move fixed-size blocks, so engines store rows in fixed-size pages (8 kB in PostgreSQL by default) and read a whole page to get one row. The buffer pool caches pages in RAM so repeated reads of hot pages cost memory time instead of a disk read.

guide.breaks: Without pages and a buffer pool every row lookup is a random disk read, and without the right row or column layout an analytics scan drags whole rows through memory to use three columns.
guide.tradeoffs: Fixed pages waste space and amplify small writes, RAM spent on the buffer pool is RAM taken from everything else, and a column store's fast scans come with slow single-row updates.
guide.explainSimply: A database keeps its data in fixed-size pages, like a warehouse that only moves whole pallets. Asking for one item still brings a pallet, so the database parks the most-used pallets by the door, which is the buffer pool. Row stores pack each order on one pallet; column stores pack all the prices together, which is better for reports.
guide.hint: Think about what the disk actually moves, and where recently used pages wait.

meow: One row? Whole page, meow. Keep the hot pages in the buffer pool and the forklift stays parked.

quiz.prompt: A PostgreSQL query fetches a single 120-byte row by primary key and nothing is cached. What does the database read from disk?
options: One 8 kB page per B-tree level it visits, then the 8 kB heap page holding the row
Only the index entry, since the index stores the row
quiz.explanation: Storage moves fixed-size pages, so each index level and the heap page cost a page read. The index entry holds a ctid, not the row, so the heap page is still needed.

quiz.prompt: A finance query sums one column across 500 million rows of a 40-column table and takes minutes on the OLTP database. Which change attacks the root cause?
options: Add a B-tree index on the summed column
Serve reporting from a column-oriented copy that reads only the columns the query needs
Increase the buffer pool until the whole table fits
Switch the table from InnoDB to MyISAM
quiz.explanation: A row store drags all 40 columns through memory to sum one; a column store reads just that column and compresses it well. A bigger buffer pool helps only if the table fits, and it still reads every row.

cards.q: Your InnoDB table uses random UUID primary keys and inserts have become slow, with many page splits. Why, and what would you change?
cards.a: InnoDB stores rows inside the primary-key B-tree, so random keys scatter inserts across the tree, dirtying many pages and splitting leaves, while increasing keys append at the right edge. Use an increasing key (auto-increment or time-ordered) and keep it short, since every secondary index copies it.

cards.q: Name the default storage engine beneath MySQL, the default beneath MongoDB, and two databases that embed RocksDB or a RocksDB-inspired engine.
cards.a: InnoDB (MySQL) and WiredTiger (MongoDB). MyRocks puts RocksDB under MySQL, and CockroachDB uses Pebble, an engine inspired by RocksDB.

glossary.note: Many small reads and writes that touch whole rows; the workload row stores are built for.
Scans and aggregates over millions of rows and a few columns; the workload column stores are built for.
